planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and provide a tall trellis or pole for the vigorous climbing vines.

directions: This family heirloom pole bean traces to seed a Russian immigrant gave to Nellie Chernoff, who grew it for decades before it was passed down and eventually shared with seed preservationists. Pick pods at about 4 to 5 inches while still tender for fresh eating; cooked pods develop a distinctive savory, umami-like richness that sets this variety apart from typical green beans. Provide sturdy 6 to 8 foot poles or a trellis, as the vines are vigorous climbers that bear over a long harvest window. Keep pods picked regularly to keep the plant productive through the season.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, and set up climbing supports before the vigorous vines take off.

directions: Czar is a British heritage runner bean distinguished by pure white flowers rather than the scarlet blooms of most runner beans, and by its dual use as both a fresh snap bean and a dry shelling bean. Young pods are broad, fleshy, and stringless when picked at 8 to 10 inches, while pods left to mature yield plump, pure-white seeds prized for drying and cooking like butter beans. Give plants a tall, sturdy trellis or bean poles and consistent moisture, since runner beans are shallow-rooted and stop setting pods readily in dry or very hot conditions. This heirloom performs especially well in cooler summer climates where heat can otherwise cause runner beans to drop blossoms.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of poles or a trellis; allow the full season for pods to dry down for shelling.

directions: Mayflower, sometimes called the Amish Knuttle Bean, is a long-cultivated heirloom pole bean grown chiefly for its small, oval seeds marked with maroon-and-white or rose speckling on a white background. Pods can be picked young as snap beans, but the variety is best known and most valued as a dry shelling bean with rich, dense flavor well suited to baking, soups, and long-simmered dishes. Train the vigorous vines up 6 to 8 foot poles or a trellis and leave pods on the plant until they rattle and the pods turn tan and papery before harvesting for storage. Its long history and vigorous, reliable production make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a dual-purpose bean with strong heirloom provenance.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after last frost; soybeans are sensitive to cold, wet soil and germinate poorly if sown too early.

directions: A popular Japanese edamame cultivar named for its traditional role as a beer-hall snack, Beer Friend produces sturdy, upright plants that concentrate their pod set for an unusually uniform, once-over harvest. Pods are plump, hold 3 to 4 large light-green beans each, and mature earlier than many edamame types, making this a good choice for shorter-season gardens. Harvest whole plants or individual clusters when pods are fully filled but still bright green, then blanch briefly and serve pods lightly salted for snacking straight from the pod. Because the crop ripens together rather than trickling in over weeks, it is well suited to a single big harvest for freezing or serving fresh.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or earliest spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop.

directions: This English heritage broad bean dates to at least the early 1800s and was nearly lost before a handful of seeds were rescued and redistributed by heirloom seed preservationists, making it as much a conservation story as a garden vegetable. Unlike the white blossoms of most fava beans, Crimson Flowered produces clusters of deep magenta-crimson flowers that make the plant genuinely ornamental as well as productive, followed by shorter, upright pods holding 3 to 4 beans each. Grow it exactly as any fava, sowing directly into cool, fertile soil and pinching growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids. Shell the beans young and tender for the best flavor, or let a portion of the crop dry fully for storage and traditional slow-cooked dishes.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; no staking needed, as this is a compact bush-type dry bean.

directions: A stabilized cross between the classic maroon-and-white Jacob's Cattle bean and a paint-type bean, this variety produces oblong white seeds dotted with striking golden-tan spots instead of the traditional dark red. Sturdy bush plants stay compact and self-supporting, bearing 4 to 5 inch pods with 6 to 8 seeds each that should be left on the plant until pods rattle and dry down fully for storage beans. The golden speckled beans hold their shape well through long cooking and take on other flavors readily, making them a favorite for baked beans, chili, and soups. Because it is bush-habit and matures reliably within a single season, it suits gardeners who want a distinctive heirloom dry bean without trellising.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm well after last frost; this heat-loving vine germinates poorly in cool soil.

directions: Distinct from the common Red Noodle type, this asparagus bean produces slender pods up to 18 inches long in a deep, glossy purple that holds its color well even after light cooking or stir-frying. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis, since vines climb vigorously and thrive in the same hot, humid conditions that stress common snap beans. Harvest pods young and pencil-thin, well before the seeds inside swell, checking plants every day or two during peak season since pods lengthen quickly. This variety tolerates heat, humidity, and many common bean pests and diseases better than Phaseolus beans, making it a reliable warm-season substitute where snap beans struggle in midsummer.
